# Steve Eisman: best and worst material takes

[Back to library](README.md)

Evidence cutoff: 2026-11-10.

The strongest material takes concern operating mechanisms and funding constraints. The weakest include identifiable forecast misses and errors in the premises used to support broader views. The examples below emphasize Eisman statements; a guest being right or wrong is credited to that guest in the episode review.

This is a reasoned selection, not a performance ranking. No brokerage record, complete position sizing, tax treatment or benchmark-relative return series was supplied.

## Strong: AI demand can be real while its financing is fragile

His distinction between strong supplier revenue and unproven downstream returns is one of the most reusable insights in the archive. In November 2025, he identified Oracle’s need for external funding because capex exceeded operating cash flow. The filings support that funding gap. This validates the balance-sheet diagnosis, not a prediction that every AI project will fail or a particular short will profit.

## Strong: power and equipment can be the bottleneck

The emphasis on turbine lead times, order books and electrical infrastructure connects AI demand to tangible constraints. Equipment demand and backlog support the operating thesis. His occasional claim that only GE Vernova and Siemens supply large turbines is wrong because Mitsubishi is a major supplier; the concentrated-market thesis survives that correction.

## A clean short-horizon success: Nvidia’s next results

On October 31, 2025, he linked higher hyperscaler spending to very strong Nvidia results at its next release. Nvidia’s November 19 release reported $57 billion revenue, up 62% year over year. This is a relatively clear, bounded operating forecast. It should not be relabeled as a successful forecast of the share-price response.

## A bounded policy success: the September 2025 quarter-point cut

In the Robert Kaplan interview, Eisman explicitly agreed with a 25-basis-point September cut rather than 50. The September 17 FOMC decision matched that call. This is an attributable Eisman forecast because he affirmatively adopted it, not simply because Kaplan was his guest. It is distinct from his earlier, unsuccessful range for total cuts during 2025.

## Supported through the cutoff: no rapid easing in 2026

In the Ives/Verrone discussion, Eisman argued that the economy was stronger than feared and the Fed was unlikely to cut quickly. Subsequent holds and a September rate increase support that direction through the audit window. Because quickly had no precise deadline, this is a bounded assessment of the observed period, not an indefinitely valid forecast.


- [Claim KByibe1S6l8-c066](episodes/youtube-KByibe1S6l8.md#KByibe1S6l8-c066)

## Strong mechanism, unfinished outcome: software refinancing

He focuses on enterprise value, sponsor equity and the lender’s decision at refinancing rather than assuming that a borrower paying interest today is safe. If enterprise value has fallen, an otherwise cash-paying borrower can still need new equity or a transfer of ownership. The mechanism is sound under its conditions; the repeatedly cited 2027 realization window remains too early to grade as a completed win.

## Promising but qualified: FICO competitive erosion

His focus on a franchise antagonizing customers and regulators through pricing identifies a real risk. GSE acceptance and aligned loan-pricing grids establish a competitive opening for VantageScore. They do not prove that aggressive pricing alone caused the reform, that application shares equal funded-loan shares, or that every earnings and stock-price target will follow. His disclosed exit is a separate position-management event.

## Useful discipline: a cheaper payment rail still needs adoption

He asks why consumers and merchants would change behavior, not just whether a transfer can be made cheaply. Rewards, acceptance, convenience and the two-sided network are real analytical obstacles to disruption. The conditional adoption point is stronger than saying Visa and Mastercard are permanently immune from competition. In the crypto interview, he also usefully separates a payment network, a stablecoin and the fee token whose owners may or may not capture value.

## Clear miss: the Supreme Court tariff forecast

On September 5, 2025, he expected the Supreme Court to uphold the tariffs because Republican justices would defer to the president. The February 20, 2026 decision rejected IEEPA tariff authority. The political shortcut failed on the specified legal issue. His separate observation that other statutes offered tariff options was supported, so the two propositions receive different grades.

## Clear miss, with tentative wording: the 2025 easing range

The July 2025 discussion allowed zero, one or two Fed cuts. By year-end, the policy-rate range was 75 basis points below July, exceeding two standard quarter-point cuts. The statement was exploratory rather than a high-conviction trade recommendation, but the stated range still missed the realized outcome.


- [Claim youtube-oycZHvqPhA8-c011](episodes/youtube-oycZHvqPhA8.md#youtube-oycZHvqPhA8-c011)

## Clear timing miss: tariffs staying on during negotiations

In the early Big Short team discussion, Eisman said tariffs would remain on for at least roughly a month while retaliation preceded talks. The April 9 order paused most country-specific reciprocal rates effective April 10, contradicting that timing for those rates; the 10% baseline and China escalation remained. His stronger claim that Trump was not interested in negotiating with China was also contradicted by the May agreement. These are more testable than a general warning that trade policy creates uncertainty.

## Clear policy miss: final Medicare Advantage rates

Eisman expected the final April 2026 announcement not to improve because of the administration’s affordability agenda. CMS instead raised the expected average payment increase from the proposed 0.09% to 2.48%. The political inference failed on the specified event. This does not itself settle insurers’ future margins, which also depend on medical costs and execution.


- [Claim jKjg_Ah8DyI-c016](episodes/youtube-jKjg_Ah8DyI.md#jKjg_Ah8DyI-c016)

## Wrong investment premise: First Solar’s manufacturing credits

In the solar discussion, Eisman says First Solar’s subsidies will be gone by 2028. The company’s subsequent filing retains Section 45X manufacturing credits through 2032, with phase-down beginning in 2030. Different solar incentives have different deadlines. This undermines a specific bearish earnings premise; it does not independently measure the guest’s short return or prove that the stock is attractive.


- [Claim xFw1WN7PVWk-c028](episodes/youtube-xFw1WN7PVWk.md#xFw1WN7PVWk-c028)

## Repeated analytical error: AI capex subtraction from GDP

The calculation multiplies a real growth rate by a nominal GDP level and subtracts a full level of AI capex to infer almost no growth outside AI. It mixes real and nominal measures, levels and changes, and spending that may include imported or non-US inputs. Concentrated AI investment could matter greatly, but this arithmetic does not quantify its contribution. Repetition is one recurring error family, not several independent failed forecasts.

## Weak explanation: valuation cannot matter until fundamentals break

His reluctance to short a good company solely because it is expensive is sensible risk management. The stronger historical claim that the internet bubble first broke because of the 2001 recession is wrong: the Nasdaq peak preceded the recession. Strong businesses can produce poor returns when expectations compress, even before a reported earnings decline.

## Technical mistakes that matter to the framework

The reviews also correct several explanations with practical consequences: a 2:1 debt-to-equity limit supports three units of assets, not two; a 90% taxable-income REIT payout is not a requirement to distribute all cash; and a one-time capital-gains tax cannot be compared directly with an annual bond yield to declare a switch mathematically irrational. These are explanation failures, distinct from losing market calls.

The financial-literacy masterclass also omits cash from enterprise value and misstates the bridges to REIT FFO and AFFO. Its decision rules are often useful, but use the standard operating-enterprise-value and Nareit FFO definitions, plus the issuer’s own AFFO reconciliation. AFFO is not standardized.

In the Dwight Collins interview, he also claims private-equity accounting permits keeping an old mark until an exit. The inspected fund disclosure instead requires current fair-value measurement. Delayed price discovery and incentives to avoid realizing losses are different from permission to ignore fair value.

## Weak explanatory area: monetary and legal mechanics

The investing Q&A says ordinary deposit rates sit above fed funds and that the Federal Reserve was created by constitutional amendment. Both premises are wrong. The episode also overstates how far house prices must fall to offset a mortgage-rate increase. These errors do not erase the useful cash-flow and stock-compensation discussion, but they make independent verification essential when the analysis moves into monetary plumbing or legal authority.

## Open investment cases: Charter and Meritage

His February 2026 purchases have explicit mechanisms: Charter capex relief and repurchases, and Meritage valuation, buybacks and possible affordability relief. They deserve continued tracking rather than premature placement in either winner or loser lists. Charter’s later subscriber and pro forma EBITDA weakness challenges the early stabilization argument; the 2029 cash-flow and longer buyback forecasts remain open. Meritage share repurchases continue, but 2026 earnings weakened and the full-year share-count forecast is unfinished.

## An important limit on criticism

A vivid interview title can sound more certain than the conversation. Consumer-collapse claims, AI extinction scenarios, biotechnology outcomes and industry price targets often belong to guests. The ledger preserves those views without silently converting them into Eisman calls. Similarly, retrospective accounts of the 2008 short do not become new forecast wins in this sample.
